# SPI Device Module Behavioral Specification

## 1. Purpose

The SPI device module is a configurable Serial Peripheral Interface slave. It provides four functional behaviors:

- A generic, full-duplex data transfer mode for exchanging raw bytes with an external SPI host.
- An SPI flash emulation mode in which the module recognizes and processes common SPI flash commands.
- An SPI passthrough mode in which the module forwards SPI traffic to a downstream SPI flash device, with optional filtering and data manipulation.
- A TPM-over-SPI mode that implements the low-level TPM command/address/data exchange protocol.

The module is programmed through a memory-mapped register interface and uses an internal memory for data buffers, command storage, read buffers, mailboxes, and TPM FIFOs.

## 2. External Behavior Overview

- The module provides an SPI slave interface with an active-low chip select, an SPI clock input, and a 4-bit bidirectional serial data bus.
- The module provides a separate active-low TPM chip select input.
- The serial data bus must be driven only when the module owns the bus for the active transaction. When no transaction is active, or when the module is not driving a particular phase, the corresponding output must be high-impedance.
- The module provides interrupt outputs for events in generic, flash, and TPM modes.
- The module provides alert output(s) for detecting integrity errors.
- The module provides an SPI clock monitor output that reflects the received SPI clock.
- The module accepts DFT/scan controls and memory configuration inputs required for implementation-level testing.

## 3. Reset and Initialization

On reset:

- All interrupt outputs must be deasserted.
- Serial data outputs must be high-impedance.
- Internal state, FIFO pointers, mode state, and configuration must return to their reset values.
- The module must not drive the SPI bus.

Software must initialize the module before use. This includes configuring the operating mode, SPI clock phase/polarity, bit order, buffer regions, command information table, interrupt enables, and TPM settings as appropriate.

Changing the operating mode while an SPI transaction is active is not supported. Mode changes should be performed when SPI activity is idle.

## 4. SPI Clock and Protocol Behavior

The module supports SPI mode 0 and SPI mode 3. The polarity and phase are software-configurable. The module must determine the sampling edge for received data and the launching edge for transmitted data from those settings.

Received and transmitted bit order are independently configurable. Each direction may be MSB-first or LSB-first.

For generic, flash, and passthrough modes, the active-low SPI chip select frames a transaction. While the chip select is active, the module must respond to SPI clock edges. When the chip select is inactive, the module must ignore SPI clock activity and must not drive the serial data outputs.

The TPM function uses the same serial data lines but a separate chip select. While the TPM chip select is active, the TPM transaction must have exclusive use of the required serial data lines.

## 5. Generic Mode

In generic mode, the module behaves as a raw byte-oriented SPI device. There is no address phase and no command decoding. Every active SPI clock edge transfers one bit in the receive direction and one bit in the transmit direction.

### 5.1 Receive Path

- Received bits must be assembled into bytes using the configured receive bit order.
- Only complete received bytes are delivered to the receive path.
- Received bytes must be written into the receive buffer in internal memory.
- The receive buffer is a circular region whose base and limit are software-configured.
- Hardware must advance the hardware-side receive write pointer as data is committed to memory.
- Software is responsible for advancing the software-side read pointer after consuming data.
- If the receive buffer is full when new data arrives, the new data must be discarded and a receive overflow condition must be reported.
- A programmable timer must force pending partial-word data to be committed to memory if a full word is not assembled within the configured time.

### 5.2 Transmit Path

- The module must read transmit data from the transmit buffer in internal memory and serialize it using the configured transmit bit order.
- The transmit buffer is a circular region whose base and limit are software-configured.
- Hardware must advance the hardware-side read pointer as data is consumed for transmission.
- Software is responsible for advancing the software-side write pointer after writing new data.
- If the transmit buffer contains no valid data when transmission is in progress, the module must continue clocking out data, but the transmitted value is unspecified. A transmit underflow condition must be reported.

### 5.3 Controls and Status

- Software must be able to reset the receive path and transmit path independently.
- Software must be able to abort ongoing generic-mode operations.
- The module must make receive and transmit buffer fullness, empty status, and depth information available to software.
- The module must generate interrupts when receive buffer full, receive watermark crossing, transmit watermark crossing, receive overflow, transmit underflow, and receive frame error conditions occur. The receive frame error event is reserved and is not asserted in the current behavior.

## 6. Flash Mode

In flash mode, the module behaves as an SPI flash device. It recognizes a set of SPI flash commands and processes them internally.

### 6.1 Command Information Table

The module maintains a software-programmable command information table. Each entry defines the behavior for a particular opcode.

The table must provide, per opcode:

- Whether the opcode is valid and recognized.
- The opcode value to match.
- Address mode: whether the address is 3 bytes, 4 bytes, or follows the current configured address mode.
- Whether address-bit manipulation is enabled.
- Whether multi-byte operation is expected.
- Dummy cycle count.
- Payload enable and payload direction.
- Whether payload-bit manipulation is enabled.
- Whether the command should be uploaded into command/address FIFOs and payload buffer.
- Whether receiving the command should set the flash status BUSY bit.

Some table entries are assigned to fixed functions:

- Read status commands.
- Read JEDEC ID command.
- Read SFDP command.
- Read commands.

Dedicated configuration is provided for the EN4B, EX4B, WREN, and WRDI opcodes.

The module must compare the first byte of an SPI transaction against the configured table. If a match is found, the module must activate the corresponding processing behavior. If no match is found and no upload behavior applies, the command should have no effect in flash mode.

### 6.2 Read Status

The module must process read status commands by returning the contents of the flash status register on the serial output.

- The status register contains a BUSY bit, a WEL bit, and additional software-controlled status bits.
- Hardware must set the BUSY bit when it receives an upload-enabled command whose command table entry has the busy attribute set.
- Software must be able to clear the BUSY bit.
- Hardware must set and clear the WEL bit when it receives the configured WREN and WRDI commands.
- Software must also be able to control the WEL bit and the other status bits.
- Software updates to the status register must be staged and made visible atomically. The staged values must be committed at chip-select deassertion so that read status commands during the same transaction observe a consistent value.

### 6.3 Read JEDEC ID

The module must process the Read JEDEC ID command by returning:

- A configurable number of continuation code bytes.
- A configurable manufacturer ID byte.
- A configurable two-byte device ID.

The manufacturer ID bytes must be sent before the device ID bytes.

### 6.4 Read SFDP

The module must process the Read SFDP command by returning data from the SFDP region of internal memory.

- The module must use the received SFDP address to index into the SFDP region.
- The upper address bits beyond the SFDP region are ignored; the address must alias into the available SFDP space.
- The module must continue returning SFDP data until the host deasserts chip select.

### 6.5 Read Commands

The module must support SPI flash read commands, including normal read, fast read, dual-output read, and quad-output read.

- The address must be received on serial data line 0.
- The address width must follow the current 3-byte/4-byte mode or the per-command address mode configuration.
- Dummy cycle count must be configurable per command.
- For dual-output and quad-output commands, the module must use the appropriate number of serial data lines for returning data.
- Data must be fetched from the read buffer in internal memory.
- If the received address falls within the configured mailbox address range and the mailbox feature is enabled, data must be fetched from the mailbox region instead of the read buffer.

The module must track the last read address for the most recent non-mailbox read command and make it visible to software after the transaction ends.

### 6.6 Read Buffer Management

The read buffer used by read commands is managed as two halves to support double buffering.

- The module must allow software to configure a read watermark.
- If a read transaction crosses the watermark, the module must generate a read watermark event.
- If a read transaction crosses from one buffer half into the other, the module must generate a buffer flip event.
- The read buffer contents are software-managed. The module must not update the read buffer contents automatically.

### 6.7 Mailbox

The mailbox region is a software-managed area of internal memory.

- The mailbox base address is software-configurable.
- The module must mask low address bits so that the mailbox is naturally aligned.
- When mailbox access is enabled and a read command address falls within the mailbox region, the module must redirect the read data source to the mailbox region.
- Mailbox accesses must not update the last read address tracking for normal read commands.

### 6.8 4-Byte Address Management

The module must support dynamic switching between 3-byte and 4-byte address modes.

- When the configured EN4B command is received, the module must switch the current address mode to 4-byte addresses.
- When the configured EX4B command is received, the module must switch the current address mode to 3-byte addresses.
- The new address mode must apply to read commands and upload commands whose address mode is configured to follow the current address mode.
- The address mode configuration must be updated in the register interface after the SPI transaction completes.
- The EN4B and EX4B opcodes are software-configurable.

### 6.9 Command Upload

For commands whose command table entry has the upload attribute enabled, the module must store the command information internally.

- The opcode must be stored in a command FIFO.
- The address, if present, must be stored in an address FIFO.
- The payload, if present, must be stored in a payload buffer.
- The module must expose the command FIFO depth, address FIFO depth, payload buffer depth, and payload start index to software.
- When a new command is uploaded, the module must generate a command FIFO not-empty event.
- When payload data is first available, the module must generate a payload not-empty event.
- If the host sends more payload than the payload buffer can hold, the module must generate a payload overflow event.
- When a payload overflow occurs, the payload start index may be nonzero. Software must handle the wrapped payload layout.

## 7. Passthrough Mode

In passthrough mode, the module forwards SPI traffic from the host side to a downstream SPI flash device and returns the downstream response to the host side.

### 7.1 Forwarding Behavior

- The module must forward SPI clock, chip select, serial data, and data-direction behavior to the downstream side.
- The downstream chip select must remain inactive whenever the host side chip select is inactive.
- The downstream path must only be active when the module is in passthrough mode and passthrough is not blocked.

### 7.2 Command Filtering

The module must be able to filter commands by opcode.

- A filter bit must exist for every possible opcode.
- If the filter bit for the received opcode is set, the module must suppress the command from reaching the downstream device.
- After receiving a filtered opcode, the module must terminate the downstream transaction by deasserting downstream chip select and stopping downstream SPI clock propagation.
- The host side transaction may continue, but the downstream device must not execute the filtered command.

### 7.3 Address Manipulation

The module must be able to modify the address portion of selected commands before forwarding them to the downstream device.

- Address manipulation applies to commands whose command table entry has address manipulation enabled.
- The manipulation is a bit-wise mask-and-overwrite operation: bits selected by the mask must be set to the values in the swap data.
- Bits not selected by the mask must pass through unchanged.

### 7.4 Payload Manipulation

The module must be able to modify the first four payload bytes of selected write commands before forwarding them.

- Payload manipulation applies to commands whose command table entry has payload manipulation enabled.
- The manipulation is a bit-wise mask-and-overwrite operation on the first four bytes.
- The bytes must be modified in transmission order: the first byte written by the host is modified first, followed by the second, third, and fourth bytes.

### 7.5 Output Enable Control

The module must control the direction of the downstream serial data bus according to the command phase.

- During opcode, address, dummy, and host-to-device payload phases, the module must drive the downstream serial data lines as required by the command and the configured I/O width.
- During device-to-host data phases, the module must stop driving the downstream data lines and sample the downstream response.
- The command information table must determine the phase lengths, lane usage, and direction for each recognized command.

For unmatched commands, the module must assume a default single-line, host-to-device payload behavior unless the opcode is filtered.

### 7.6 Internal Command Interception

In passthrough mode, the module may be configured to intercept certain commands and respond internally instead of forwarding them.

- Read status, Read JEDEC ID, Read SFDP, and mailbox-region read commands can be intercepted.
- Interception must be individually enableable.
- When a command is intercepted, the module must generate the response internally on the host side and must not forward the command to the downstream device.
- Software should filter intercepted commands to prevent the downstream device from also seeing them.

### 7.7 Passthrough Blocking

The passthrough path must be blocked while the flash status BUSY bit is set.

- The block must be applied while the SPI transaction is idle, before a new passthrough transaction begins.
- The module must not forward a new transaction to the downstream device while BUSY is set.
- When software clears BUSY, normal passthrough operation may resume.

## 8. TPM Mode

The TPM function provides a TPM-over-SPI protocol interface using a dedicated TPM chip select.

TPM mode can be active together with flash mode or passthrough mode. It is not supported together with generic mode. The host must not issue a TPM transaction and a normal SPI transaction at the same time because the serial data lines are shared.

### 8.1 TPM Transaction Capture

- When the TPM chip select is active, the module must sample the incoming serial data using the SPI clock.
- The first byte received is the TPM command byte.
- The next three bytes received are the TPM address.
- The module must store the command and address in a command/address buffer for software processing, unless the transaction is handled by hardware as described below.

### 8.2 TPM Read Behavior

For a TPM read transaction:

- The module must determine whether the requested address corresponds to a return-by-hardware register.
- Return-by-hardware registers are a defined set of TPM register addresses whose values are supplied by the TPM configuration registers.
- If the requested address is a return-by-hardware register and hardware register returns are enabled, the module must return the register value directly to the host. In this case, the command and address must not be pushed to the software-visible command/address buffer.
- If the address is not hardware-returned, or if the mode is CRB mode, the module must use the read FIFO. The module must send WAIT until software has written enough data into the read FIFO. When data is available, the module must send START and then transmit the read FIFO contents.
- The module must handle locality information from the address and the activeLocality status to select the appropriate return register value.
- If invalid locality is configured and the address uses an unsupported locality, the module must return the appropriate invalid response.

### 8.3 TPM Write Behavior

For a TPM write transaction:

- The module must store the command and address in the command/address buffer.
- The module must accept the payload bytes and store them in the write FIFO.
- If the write FIFO is not available, the module must send WAIT until the write FIFO becomes available.
- Once the write FIFO is available, the module must send START and then accept the payload bytes.
- The write FIFO is read by software. The module must expose the write FIFO data and depth status to software.

### 8.4 TPM Mode Configuration

- The module must support FIFO mode and CRB mode.
- In FIFO mode, hardware return of the defined registers is permitted with at most one wait state.
- In CRB mode, hardware return of the defined registers should not be used; the module must always rely on software-provided read FIFO data.
- Software must be able to configure the TPM capability values, including supported revision, locality, and maximum read/write sizes.
- The module must make the TPM command/address buffer not-empty status visible to software. This status is level-sensitive and remains asserted until the buffer is emptied.

### 8.5 TPM Register Interface Behavior

- The module must expose software-writable configuration and status registers for the return-by-hardware TPM registers.
- Software must not update the return-by-hardware register contents while a TPM transaction is active.
- The module must latch or otherwise use the configured register values when the TPM transaction begins.

## 9. Interrupt Behavior

The module must provide individual interrupt outputs for the following events:

- Generic mode receive buffer full.
- Generic mode receive watermark reached.
- Generic mode transmit watermark reached.
- Generic mode receive frame error.
- Generic mode receive overflow.
- Generic mode transmit underflow.
- Upload command FIFO not empty.
- Upload payload not empty.
- Upload payload overflow.
- Read buffer watermark crossed.
- Read buffer half flipped.
- TPM command/address buffer not empty.

Each interrupt output must be controlled by the corresponding interrupt enable and interrupt test registers. Interrupt status must be software-readable and software-clearable according to the standard interrupt scheme.

The TPM command/address buffer not-empty interrupt is level-sensitive. It must remain asserted while the underlying condition is true, regardless of software clearing the interrupt status, until the condition is removed.

The upload command FIFO and upload payload not-empty interrupts may be edge-triggered events that pulse when the corresponding FIFO or buffer transitions from empty to non-empty.

## 10. Alerts and Reliability

The module must detect bus integrity errors on the register interface.

- When an integrity error is detected, the module must assert the alert output.
- The module must provide a software-accessible alert test mechanism so software can verify alert propagation.
- Alert behavior must comply with the configured asynchronous alert mode.

The internal memory is protected with parity. Read operations from software that encounter a parity error must be reported as an error response on the memory access path.

## 11. DFT and Clock Monitoring

The module must provide the received SPI clock value on a dedicated SPI clock monitor output for use by an external clock monitor.

The module must accept DFT control inputs for scan testing and memory BIST:

- When scan mode is activated, the functional SPI clock and reset paths must be overridable by the scan clock and scan reset.
- When memory BIST is activated, the internal memory clock must be overridable by the BIST clock.
- DFT controls must not affect normal functional behavior when disabled.

The memory configuration input must be applied to the internal memory array so that the memory behaves according to the configured compiled memory settings.

# SPI Passthrough Behavioral Specification

## 1. Overview

The SPI passthrough function forwards SPI traffic from an external host to a downstream SPI flash device while providing three protective features:

- Command filtering: prohibited commands are terminated before they can affect the downstream device.
- Address manipulation: selected address bits may be replaced with software-provided values, enabling A/B image selection.
- Payload manipulation: selected bits in the first four bytes of a host-to-flash payload may be replaced with software-provided values.

The module also controls the direction of the SPI data lines so that the host and downstream flash device never drive the same line simultaneously.

## 2. Activation and Transaction Framing

The passthrough behavior shall be active only when the selected SPI mode is passthrough and the passthrough block control is not asserted. When passthrough is not active or is blocked, the module shall not perform filtering, address substitution, or payload substitution, and shall not claim ownership of the SPI transaction.

A transaction begins when the host asserts its chip-select. The module shall treat the first complete byte on the incoming single data line as the opcode. The opcode shall be evaluated after all eight bits have been received.

The module shall consider the transaction complete when the host releases chip-select. It shall return to an idle state at that point and be ready for the next transaction. If chip-select is released at any time, the module shall stop driving the downstream interface and shall not continue processing the transaction.

## 3. Command Filtering

A 256-bit filter vector is provided. Each bit position corresponds to one opcode value. If the bit corresponding to the received opcode is set, the command is prohibited.

When a prohibited command is received:

- The transaction to the downstream flash device shall be terminated at the opcode boundary.
- Downstream chip-select shall be forced to its inactive state.
- Downstream SPI clock shall be stopped so that no further bits of the prohibited command are delivered to the downstream device.
- The module shall remain in this terminated state until the host releases chip-select.
- The module shall assert an event output to indicate that a command was filtered.

Filtering shall take priority over any command descriptor information. A command with a set filter bit shall never be forwarded to the downstream device, even if a command descriptor exists for that opcode.

## 4. Command Descriptor Handling

The module is provided with a set of command descriptors. A descriptor describes how a particular opcode shall be handled after the opcode byte: whether it has an address phase, how many address bytes are used, whether dummy cycles are present, whether payload data is input or output, which SPI lanes are active during the payload phase, and whether address or payload substitution is enabled.

When a received opcode matches a valid descriptor:

- The module shall follow the descriptor for the remainder of the transaction.
- Address substitution, dummy-cycle handling, payload direction, and output-enable control shall be performed according to that descriptor.

When a received opcode does not match any descriptor and is not filtered, the module shall treat the transaction as a single-lane host-to-flash payload command. In this case, all bits after the opcode shall be forwarded to the downstream device unchanged.

## 5. Address Phase and Address Manipulation

For commands with an address phase, the module shall forward the address from the host to the downstream device.

The address phase length shall be:

- 24 bits when 4-byte address mode is disabled.
- 32 bits when 4-byte address mode is enabled.

Command descriptors with a fixed address length may override this selection where appropriate.

If the command descriptor enables address substitution, selected address bits may be replaced while the address is being forwarded. The substitution is controlled by a 32-bit mask and a 32-bit data word.

For each address bit:

- If the corresponding mask bit is 1, the downstream device shall receive the value from the data word instead of the host value.
- If the corresponding mask bit is 0, the downstream device shall receive the host value unchanged.

The first address bit transferred shall correspond to the most significant address bit: bit 23 for a 24-bit address, or bit 31 for a 32-bit address. Address substitution applies to address bits received on the single data line only. Multi-lane address phases are not supported for substitution.

## 6. Dummy and Mode Phases

If the command descriptor indicates dummy cycles, the module shall wait for the configured number of dummy cycles before enabling the payload phase.

During the dummy phase:

- The module shall not drive data to the downstream device.
- The module shall not return data to the host.
- All SPI data lines shall remain high-impedance.

After the dummy phase completes, the module shall continue based on the payload direction indicated by the descriptor.

## 7. Payload Phase and Payload Manipulation

For host-to-flash payload commands, the module shall forward the payload from the host to the downstream device. For flash-to-host payload commands, the module shall forward the returned payload from the downstream device to the host.

If the command descriptor enables payload substitution, and the payload direction is host-to-flash, the module shall replace selected bits in the first four payload bytes. The replacement is controlled by a 32-bit mask and a 32-bit data word.

For each payload bit in the first four bytes:

- If the corresponding mask bit is 1, the downstream device shall receive the value from the data word instead of the host value.
- If the corresponding mask bit is 0, the downstream device shall receive the host value unchanged.

The 32-bit mask/data word is consumed in transmission order from the most significant bit to the least significant bit. Therefore:

- Bits [31:24] correspond to the first payload byte.
- Bits [23:16] correspond to the second payload byte.
- Bits [15:8] correspond to the third payload byte.
- Bits [7:0] correspond to the fourth payload byte.

Payload substitution shall affect only the first four bytes of the payload. Bytes after the fourth byte shall be forwarded unchanged.

Payload substitution is intended for single-lane host-to-flash payloads. It shall only be considered valid when the descriptor indicates a single active payload lane and the payload direction is host-to-flash.

## 8. Output-Enable and Line-Direction Control

The module shall control the direction of the SPI data lines on both the host side and the downstream side so that there is no contention.

The behavior shall be as follows:

- While the host is sending opcode, address, dummy, or host-to-flash payload bits, the downstream-facing data lines shall be driven for the active lanes, and the host-facing data lines shall be high-impedance.
- While the downstream device is returning flash-to-host payload data, the host-facing data lines shall be driven for the active lanes, and the downstream-facing data lines shall be high-impedance.
- During dummy phases, neither side shall drive the data lines.
- For multi-lane payload phases, only the lanes indicated by the command descriptor shall be driven. All other lanes shall remain high-impedance.

The module shall continue driving the appropriate data line direction for the entire transaction until the host releases chip-select.

## 9. Downstream SPI Clock and Chip-Select Behavior

The module shall forward the host SPI clock to the downstream device while a permitted transaction is in progress. The polarity of the downstream SPI clock shall match the configured clock polarity.

The downstream SPI clock must be glitch-free. When a command is filtered, the downstream SPI clock shall be disabled before any further data is clocked into the downstream device.

Downstream chip-select shall follow the host chip-select during normal permitted transactions. When a command is filtered, the downstream chip-select shall be forced inactive and shall remain inactive until the host releases its chip-select.

The module shall ensure that downstream chip-select transitions are glitch-free and that downstream chip-select deassertion is not ambiguous to the downstream flash device.

## 10. Event Indication

The module shall provide an event output that is asserted when an incoming command is filtered. This event shall be generated for every filtered command and shall not be generated for commands that are forwarded normally.

## 11. Summary of Required Behavior

- Forward host SPI traffic to the downstream flash device in passthrough mode.
- Terminate and block any command whose filter bit is set.
- Substitute configured address bits during read-type address phases.
- Substitute configured payload bits during the first four bytes of host-to-flash payload.
- Control data-line direction according to command phase and configured payload lanes.
- Preserve normal SPI protocol timing, clock polarity, and chip-select framing for all permitted transactions.
- Return to idle after the host releases chip-select and be ready for the next transaction.
